extracted.intended_audience: district court judges, trial lawyers, and juries in U.S. patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions setting forth the legal standards for patent infringement (direct, indirect, foreign-supply theories, multiparticipant scenarios, willfulness) and for validity challenges (burden of proof, written description, enablement, prior art/anticipation, obviousness). Intended to guide judges in instructing juries and attorneys in framing issues at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for contributory infringement of a claim if [patent holder] proves by a preponderance of the evidence:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements (must prove each by a preponderance): (1) [alleged infringer] sells, offers to sell, or imports within the United States a component of a product, or apparatus for use in a process, during the time the [ ] patent is in force; (2) the component or apparatus has no substantial, noninfringing use; (3) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the invention; (4) [alleged infringer] is aware of the [ ] patent and knows that the [products or processes] for which the [component or apparatus] has no other substantial use may be covered by a claim of the [ ] patent or may satisfy a claim of the [ ] patent under the doctrine of equivalents; and (5) that use directly infringes the claim. Proof standard: preponderance of the evidence. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(c); Aro Mfg. Co. v. Convertible Top Replacement Co., Ricoh v. Quanta, Alloc, Mentor H/S, Hewlett-Packard v. Bausch & Lomb, Preemption Devices v. Minn. Mining & Mfg., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: §271(f)(1) — infringement by supplying components from the U.S. for combination abroad (active inducement)
rubrics_metrics.description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for §271(f)(1) infringement if patentee proves by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) [alleged infringer] supplies [or causes to be supplied] components from the United States to a place outside the United States, which make up all or a substantial portion of the invention of any one of the claims; (2) [alleged infringer] takes action intentionally to cause another to assemble the components outside the United States; (3) [alleged infringer] knows of the [ ] patent, and knows that the encouraged acts constitute infringement of that patent; and (4) the encouraged acts would constitute direct infringement if carried out in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant believed the acts encouraged would not constitute infringement if carried out in the United States, the defendant cannot be liable for inducement. Mere awareness that the alleged direct infringer itself infringes or awareness of the acts is insufficient — must find that defendant specifically intended for the other to infringe. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(1); cases include Cardiac Pacemakers, Microsoft v. AT&T, Liquid Dynamics, Pellegrini, NTP v. RIM, Union Carbide, Waymark. Committee comment: instruction omits 'willful blindness' standard (Global-Tech) for simplicity; include when patentee proceeds on that theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: §271(f)(2) — contributory foreign infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for §271(f)(2) infringement if [patent holder] proves by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) [alleged infringer] supplies, or causes a component to be supplied, from the United States to a place outside the United States; (2) the only substantial use for the component is in a product that would infringe if the combination had occurred in the United States; (3) [alleged infringer] is aware of the [ ] patent and knows that the [component or apparatus] has no other substantial use and may be covered by a claim [literally or under the doctrine of equivalents]; and (4) intends for the component to be used in a product that would directly infringe the claim if used in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(f); relevant Federal Circuit decisions cited in the instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: §271(g) — infringement by import/sale/use of product made abroad by patented process
rubrics_metrics.description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for direct infringement if [patent holder] proves by a preponderance that [alleged infringer], without authorization, imports, offers to sell, sells, or uses within the United States a product which was made outside of the United States by a process that, if performed in the United States, would infringe the claim literally or under the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if the product has been materially changed by an additional process or has become a trivial and nonessential component of another product, there is no infringement. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(g); Bayer AG v. Housey, Ajinomoto v. Archer-Daniels-Midland.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement when one or more system components are located outside the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: When some (but not all) elements of a claimed system are located outside the United States, [patent holder] must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the control of the system was exercised and the benefit of the system was enjoyed in the United States for infringement to occur within the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct infringement requires that the accused system include every element recited in the claim; to find infringement in the U.S. the place where the system is put into service must be where control is exercised and beneficial use obtained. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(a); NTP, Inc. v. Research in Motion, Ltd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement by combined acts of multiple parties (joint enterprise or direction/control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement occurs where all steps of a claimed method are performed by or attributable to a single party. If more than one party is involved, infringement may exist only if the acts of one are attributable to the other because they formed a joint enterprise or one party directed or controlled the other's performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish infringement by multiple parties, patentee must prove by a preponderance: (1) all steps were performed in the United States; and (2) acts of party B are attributable to party A either because (a) A and B formed a joint enterprise, or (b) A directed or controlled B's acts. Elements to prove a joint enterprise (patentee must prove all four): (1) agreement (express or implied) between parties; (2) shared common purpose; (3) each had a financial interest in that purpose; and (4) each had an equal right of control. To prove direction/control: show B performed claim steps to receive a benefit from A and that A established how or when the steps were performed. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(a); Limelight Networks v. Akamai.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement (enhanced damages standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Willfulness requires clear and convincing evidence that [alleged infringer] acted recklessly. If infringement is found, the jury must determine whether the infringement was willful by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-part test (must prove both by clear and convincing evidence): (A) Objective prong: whether defendant acted despite a high likelihood that its actions infringed a valid and enforceable patent — this prong is objective and the jury may not consider defendant's state of mind; legitimate/credible defenses demonstrate lack of recklessness. (B) Subjective prong (only considered if objective prong met): whether defendant actually knew or should have known that its actions constituted an unjustifiably high risk of infringement. Consider nonexhaustive factors including: (1) whether defendant acted in accordance with industry standards; (2) whether defendant intentionally copied a product covered by the patent; (3) whether there was a reasonable basis to believe defendant did not infringe or had a reasonable defense; (4) whether defendant made a good-faith effort to avoid infringement (e.g., attempted design-around); (5) whether defendant tried to cover up infringement. Opinion-of-counsel defense: if relied on, jury should evaluate whether the opinion was of sufficient quality that reliance was reasonable. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 284; In re Seagate; Knorr-Bremse; Crystal Semiconductor; WMS Gaming; Read; Gustafson. Committee comment: judge should consider deciding objective prong as a question of law when appropriate; some pattern instructions omit listing nonexhaustive factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity—burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that any claim of a patent is invalid, [alleged infringer] must persuade you by clear and convincing evidence, i.e., you must be left with a clear conviction that the claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are presumed valid under 35 U.S.C. § 282; invalidity may be asserted under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112, or 251. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 282; Microsoft Corp. v. i4i; Schumer v. Lab. Computer Sys.; Buildex; Hybritech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: [Alleged infringer] contends claims are invalid because the specification does not contain an adequate written description. To succeed, [alleged infringer] must show by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: from the viewpoint of a person having ordinary skill in the field at the time of filing, the written description requirement is satisfied if that person would have recognized that the original application describes the full scope of the claimed invention and that the inventor actually possessed that full scope by the filing date. The written description may be satisfied by any combination of words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, etc.; explicit disclosure of every claim term is not required if a person skilled in the art would understand the disclosure to include the claimed scope. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶¶ 1,2; Ariad (en banc); Lizard Tech.; Univ. of Rochester; Chiron; Purdue; Lampi; Gentry Gallery; Regents of Univ. of Cal.; In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: [Alleged infringer] contends claims are invalid because the specification does not contain a sufficiently full and clear description of how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention (enablement). To succeed, [alleged infringer] must show by clear and convincing evidence the patent does not contain a sufficiently full and clear description enabling the full scope of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement requires disclosure sufficient for a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation. Some experimentation is allowable. Factors (Wands factors) to consider in determining undue experimentation (no single factor dispositive): (1) time and cost of necessary experimentation; (2) how routine experimentation is in the field; (3) whether the patent discloses specific working examples; (4) amount of guidance in the patent; (5) nature and predictability of the field; (6) level of ordinary skill in the field; (7) scope of the claimed invention. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 1; Sitrick v. Dreamworks; Auto. Techs. Int’l v. BMW; AK Steel; Union Pac. Res.; Ajinomoto; In re Wands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode (removed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'best mode' instruction has been removed; failure to disclose the best mode is no longer a basis for invalidity or unenforceability under the America Invents Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction was removed because section 15 of the America Invents Act (effective Sept. 16, 2011) eliminated best mode as a basis for invalidity or unenforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (effective filing date before March 16, 2013) and anticipation definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art may include items publicly known, used, on sale, or printed publications or patents that disclose the claimed invention or elements. To be prior art, the item must have been made, known, used, published, or patented either before the invention was made or [insert date if undisputed] or more than one year before the filing date. For anticipation, [alleged infringer] must show by clear and convincing evidence that all the requirements of the claim were present in a single previous device or method known, used, or described in a single printed publication or patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art exclusions: a publication that describes the inventor’s own work is not prior art if published less than one year before the date of invention. For anticipation, the prior reference need not use the same words, but must disclose all claim limitations expressly or inherently such that a person skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 102 (pre-AIA); relevant Federal Circuit authorities cited in the instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention date / conception and reduction to practice (when in dispute)
rubrics_metrics.description: If invention date is disputed, the jury must determine the date of invention (conception and/or reduction to practice) for the claimed invention or alleged prior art. Conception is the formation in the mind of a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention; reduction to practice occurs when constructed/used/tested sufficiently to show it will work or when a patent application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence: conception is effective only if followed by diligence in reducing to practice; diligence means working continuously though not necessarily every day. Conception may be evidenced by drawings, disclosure to another, or other evidence beyond the inventor's testimony. Reduction to practice may be shown by prototype or by a filed patent application. Authorities and examples provided in instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation and loss of right to patent — specific non-novelty grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Ways a patentee can lose rights or a claim can be not new (patentee must be convinced by clear and convincing evidence):
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated items (choose applicable ones): (1) invention known to or used by others in the U.S. before the date of invention; (2) already patented or described in a printed publication anywhere before the date of invention; (3) patentee lost rights if claim was patented or described in a printed publication more than a year before effective filing date; (4) publicly used, sold, or offered for sale in the U.S. more than one year before the effective filing date; (5) abandonment; (6) foreign patenting or earlier foreign filing more than one year before U.S. filing; (7) described in a published patent application by another in the U.S. before date of invention; (8) described in a patent granted on an application filed by another before the relevant date; (9) patentee did not himself invent the invention; (10) another made the invention in the U.S. before patentee and did not abandon, suppress, or conceal it. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)-(g) and multiple Federal Circuit decisions cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013 — AIA rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents with effective filing dates on or after March 16, 2013, prior art may include: (1) items publicly known or used, on sale, or otherwise made available to the public before the filing date; (2) publications made available to the public before the filing date; and (3) patents and published patent applications naming another inventor filed before the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluded from prior art: an item/publication that is the inventor’s own work or obtained from the inventor unless made public more than one year before filing; a patent or application that discloses the inventor's own work or was obtained from/owned by the same person. Anticipation standard (single reference must disclose all claim limitations expressly or inherently so that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention) still applies. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1)-(2); 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)-(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: [Alleged infringer] may establish that a patent claim is invalid by showing by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention would have been obvious to persons having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made or the patent was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining obviousness, consider: the level of ordinary skill in the field at the relevant time; the scope and content of the prior art; and any differences between the prior art and the claimed invention. The obviousness inquiry requires a factual assessment of these considerations and legal application to invalidate claims. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 103 and related case law cited in the instructions.
